transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Um, well, what brings me in is I just... I cannot seem to keep my work in order anymore. I work at a dry cleaner, and it's just getting to be too much. The tickets, the receipts, workshop notes, customer jobs—it's all just piled together until I honestly do not know what to handle first. It's embarrassing, really. Just the other day, Mrs. Gable came in—she’s this lovely older lady who always brings in these beautiful silk scarves, you know the kind with the hand-rolled edges? Anyway, she came in to pick up her husband’s suits, and I couldn't find the ticket. I spent twenty minutes looking for it, and it turned out it was stuck to the bottom of a box of hangers. I don't even know how it got there. My husband says I should just use a different filing system, but he doesn't get how fast-paced it is. He works in construction, so it's all just big tools and dirt, not a million tiny pieces of paper... but yeah, I just can't keep things straight anymore.
Have you struggled with this kind of disorganization and difficulty focusing since you were a child, or is this something that's only started recently?

Oh, it's definitely not new. I mean, even back in grade school, my teachers were always telling my mother that I was bright but scattered. Always talking out of turn, losing my papers, needing constant reminders just to finish whatever worksheet we were supposed to be doing. I remember one time in third grade—Mrs. Higgins was my teacher, she had this huge collection of ceramic frogs on her desk, like everywhere you looked, frogs—and she got so mad at me because I lost my permission slip for the field trip to the zoo. I wanted to see the giraffes so badly, they're my favorite animal, just so graceful, you know? But I couldn't go until my mom had to drive all the way to the school to sign a new one because I'd stuffed the original one in my desk and it just vanished into the black hole of crumpled papers. My mom was furious, she had to leave work early and she was working at this diner at the time, smelling like French fries... but yeah, no, it's been like this my whole life. Just always a mess.
Do you often feel restless, fidgety, or find yourself acting or speaking impulsively—like interrupting others or having trouble sitting still—separate from the disorganization you described?

Well, I don't know about interrupting people, but sitting still is... it's really hard for me. Like, whenever we have those church committee meetings—I'm on the hospitality committee, we organize the coffee hours after service, which is a lot of work, by the way. People think you just plug in the percolator and put out some store-bought cookies, but no, we try to have a nice spread. Marge usually brings her lemon bars, which are just to die for, though I think she uses way too much powdered sugar on top. It gets all over your nice Sunday clothes. But anyway, during those meetings, or even during the fabric-care trainings we have to do for work—which are so boring, honestly, how many ways can you talk about spot-treating silk?—I just can't stay in my chair. I'm always finding a reason to get up. I'll go get a glass of water, or I'll pretend I need to grab a pen, or check on something in the other room. Everybody else is just sitting there perfectly fine, listening, and I'm up and down like a jack-in-the-box. I just feel this... this buzz in my legs and I have to move. I tried wearing those compression socks once, thinking maybe it was my circulation? My sister-in-law swears by them, she's a nurse at the county hospital, works twelve-hour shifts on her feet all day... but yeah, no, the socks didn't help at all. I just have to get up.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient endorses a lifelong (since grade school) pattern of both prominent inattentive symptoms (disorganization, losing important items, difficulty prioritizing tasks, distractibility) and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (inability to remain seated, restlessness/'buzzing' in legs, excessive movement in structured settings). Symptoms are pervasive across multiple settings (childhood school, workplace, church committee, trainings) and have caused functional impairment (occupational difficulties, embarrassment, disciplinary issues in childhood). The combination of significant inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms meeting criteria in both domains, present since childhood and persisting into adulthood, supports the Combined Presentation (F90.2) rather than a predominantly inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive subtype.
